# Word-Client — Premium Cross-Platform Desktop Word Processor

Build a professional, premium desktop word processor named **Word-Client**.

The application must be designed for Linux, Windows, and macOS. It should be suitable for commercial distribution as paid software.

The goal is to create a genuinely useful desktop word processor inspired by Microsoft Word, with a professional editing experience, strong document compatibility, polished native desktop behavior, and a maintainable architecture.

Do not build a website, landing page, dashboard mockup, or a simple text editor disguised as a word processor.

## 1. Product Identity

Application name: Word-Client  
Project directory: word-client  
Application window title: Word-Client  
Product type: Cross-platform desktop word processor  
Target platforms:
- Linux
- Windows
- macOS

The product should feel like a premium desktop productivity application.

Use Microsoft Word Online as a visual and interaction reference where available, but create an original product identity.

Do not use Microsoft's official branding, logo, proprietary assets, or claim that this application is an official Microsoft product.

## 2. Cross-Platform Requirements

The application must be designed to run on:

### Linux
- Support common Linux desktop environments.
- Prioritize compatibility with Debian-based distributions, including Kali Linux and Ubuntu.
- Provide a native desktop application experience.
- Support appropriate application menus, file dialogs, keyboard shortcuts, window management, and desktop integration.
- Plan packaging for AppImage and Debian packages where feasible.

### Windows
- Support modern Windows desktop environments.
- Provide a native application window.
- Support standard Windows file dialogs and keyboard shortcuts.
- Plan packaging as an installable Windows application.

### macOS
- Support modern macOS desktop environments.
- Provide native-feeling window behavior.
- Respect macOS keyboard conventions.
- Support standard macOS file dialogs and application menus.
- Plan packaging as a macOS application bundle.

Do not make the application Linux-specific.

Do not hardcode Linux paths, shell commands, or Linux-only functionality into the core application.

Use platform-aware APIs and abstractions for filesystem access, application menus, window behavior, file dialogs, and application storage.

## 3. Technology Stack

Use the following architecture:

### Desktop framework
Tauri 2.

Use Tauri for:
- Desktop application windows
- Native filesystem integration
- Native file dialogs
- Application menus
- Desktop packaging
- Secure communication between the frontend and backend

### Frontend
- React
- TypeScript
- Vite
- Tailwind CSS

### Document editing engine
Use Tiptap with ProseMirror as the document editing foundation.

Design the editor around a structured document model rather than a plain HTML textarea.

Use a modular editor architecture so document features can be added without rewriting the application.

### Backend
Use Rust for Tauri backend functionality.

Use the backend for operations that require native filesystem access, platform integration, or document processing.

Do not put all document processing into frontend components.

## 4. Architecture Before Implementation

Before implementing the complete application:

1. Inspect the existing project directory.
2. Determine whether the repository already contains an application.
3. Preserve useful existing code.
4. Identify the current framework, dependencies, and project structure.
5. Create a clear implementation plan.
6. Establish the application architecture.
7. Identify document format limitations.
8. Identify platform-specific requirements.
9. Implement the application in organized, maintainable stages.

Do not blindly overwrite existing project files.

Do not create a new project inside another unnecessary nested directory.

Keep the application source in the existing word-client project directory.

## 5. Main Application Interface

Create a professional desktop word processor interface.

The interface should include:

### Application window
- Application title
- Main menu
- Document workspace
- Editing toolbar
- Document status information
- Appropriate desktop window behavior

### Main menu

Provide menus for:

File:
- New document
- Open document
- Open recent document
- Save
- Save as
- Export
- Print
- Close document

Edit:
- Undo
- Redo
- Cut
- Copy
- Paste
- Select all
- Find
- Replace

Insert:
- Table
- Image
- Link
- Page break
- Header
- Footer
- Page number

Format:
- Font
- Paragraph
- Alignment
- Line spacing
- Indentation
- Lists

View:
- Zoom
- Page layout
- Ruler
- Navigation panel
- Full-screen mode

Tools:
- Word count
- Spell checking
- Document settings

Help:
- About Word-Client
- Keyboard shortcuts
- Documentation

Only implement menu items when their functionality exists.

Do not create decorative menu items that do nothing.

## 6. Document Editing

The document editor is the core of Word-Client.

Implement a structured rich-text editing experience.

Required editing features:

- Text input
- Text selection
- Undo and redo
- Copy and paste
- Bold
- Italic
- Underline
- Strikethrough
- Font family
- Font size
- Text color
- Text highlighting
- Paragraph alignment
- Left alignment
- Center alignment
- Right alignment
- Justified alignment
- Line spacing
- Paragraph spacing
- Indentation
- Bulleted lists
- Numbered lists
- Headings
- Hyperlinks
- Tables
- Images
- Page breaks

Use a structured document model.

Do not rely on a single contenteditable element with custom formatting hacks.

Formatting must persist when documents are saved and reopened.

## 7. Document Page Layout

The editor should resemble a professional page-based word processor.

Implement:

- White document pages
- Document margins
- Page boundaries
- Page background
- Editable document content
- Page numbering support
- Page navigation
- Zoom controls
- Document width controls
- A workspace surrounding the document

The page layout should be suitable for writing reports, letters, assignments, proposals, and professional documents.

Do not make the editor look like a chat application or a generic dashboard.

Avoid excessive cards, floating panels, gradients, decorative borders, and oversized typography.

Prioritize the document itself.

### Page rendering

Investigate a reliable approach for rendering and editing multi-page documents.

Avoid pretending that a single scrolling contenteditable element provides complete Microsoft Word-style pagination.

Clearly separate:
- Document structure
- Editing behavior
- Page layout
- Rendering
- Export behavior

Ensure the implementation is maintainable.

## 8. Document File Support

Support local documents.

### Required formats

DOCX:
- Open existing `.docx` documents.
- Preserve supported formatting.
- Edit imported content.
- Save documents as `.docx`.
- Export documents as `.docx`.

TXT:
- Open plain text files.
- Save plain text files.

HTML:
- Support importing or exporting HTML where practical.

PDF:
- Support PDF export.
- Support printing through the platform where practical.

### DOCX compatibility

DOCX support is a major product requirement.

Use a suitable document conversion or processing library.

Investigate the best reliable implementation for:
- Importing DOCX
- Exporting DOCX
- Preserving paragraphs
- Preserving headings
- Preserving text formatting
- Preserving lists
- Preserving tables
- Preserving images
- Preserving hyperlinks
- Preserving page-related properties

Do not claim full Microsoft Word compatibility unless it has been implemented and tested.

Do not silently discard unsupported document elements.

Where possible, preserve unsupported content or provide a clear warning.

Keep the document model extensible so compatibility can improve over time.

## 9. File Operations

Implement real filesystem functionality.

Required features:

- Create document
- Open document
- Save document
- Save as
- Open recent documents
- Rename where appropriate
- Export document
- Print document
- Detect unsaved changes
- Warn before closing unsaved documents
- Handle file permission errors
- Handle missing files
- Handle invalid document files
- Handle failed saves

Use native file dialogs through Tauri.

Do not hardcode the user's home directory.

Do not assume that Linux, Windows, and macOS use the same filesystem paths.

Implement autosave carefully.

Autosave should not overwrite the user's original document unexpectedly.

Use a reliable document recovery strategy.

## 10. Document Recovery

Implement a recovery mechanism for unsaved work.

Requirements:
- Maintain recovery data for unsaved documents.
- Restore recoverable work after unexpected application termination.
- Avoid corrupting original files.
- Clearly indicate recovered documents.
- Allow users to discard recovery data.
- Avoid storing document contents in an insecure or unnecessary location.

Use platform-appropriate application data directories.

Do not hardcode temporary file paths.

## 11. Cloud Integration

Design the application so cloud storage can be added without making cloud services mandatory.

Potential integration:
- Microsoft OneDrive
- Microsoft Graph API
- Microsoft account authentication

Use Microsoft Graph API for authorized access to supported Microsoft cloud files.

Use the Microsoft identity platform for authentication.

Implement OAuth securely.

Do not store passwords directly.

Do not embed confidential client secrets in the application.

Do not assume that Microsoft Graph provides access to Microsoft's proprietary Word editing engine.

Do not attempt to recreate Microsoft's internal document rendering service through undocumented APIs.

Cloud integration must not prevent users from opening and editing local documents.

The application should remain useful offline.

If cloud functionality is not fully implemented, clearly identify it as a planned feature rather than presenting a fake working integration.

## 12. User Interface

Create a premium, restrained productivity interface.

Design principles:
- Professional
- Clean
- Efficient
- Desktop-oriented
- Consistent
- Accessible
- Responsive to window resizing

Use a compact toolbar.

Provide a clear hierarchy between:
- Application menus
- Formatting controls
- Document workspace
- Navigation
- Status information

Use a light theme and a dark theme.

### Light theme
Use a clean professional document editing appearance.

### Dark theme
Use a comfortable dark application interface.

The document page may remain white in dark mode unless a user-configurable page appearance is implemented.

Do not force dark document backgrounds into exported documents.

Implement theme persistence.

Use system theme detection where practical.

Do not create fake theme controls.

## 13. Typography

Provide a practical font selection system.

Support:
- Font family
- Font size
- Bold
- Italic
- Underline
- Text color
- Highlight color

Use fonts available on the user's system.

Do not assume that proprietary Microsoft fonts are installed.

Handle missing fonts gracefully.

Where font substitution occurs, avoid corrupting the original document's formatting.

## 14. Toolbar

Create a professional editing toolbar with functional controls.

Include:
- Undo
- Redo
- Font selection
- Font size
- Bold
- Italic
- Underline
- Text color
- Highlight
- Alignment
- Lists
- Insert link
- Insert table
- Insert image
- Zoom

Toolbar controls must reflect the current selection.

When the user selects bold text, the bold button should indicate its active state.

When the user changes font size, the document content should actually change.

When the user inserts a table, create a real editable table.

Do not implement controls that only change their appearance without affecting the document.

## 15. Navigation and Status

Implement a document navigation panel.

Where appropriate, provide:
- Document outline
- Heading navigation
- Find
- Replace
- Page navigation
- Word count
- Character count
- Current page
- Total page count
- Zoom percentage

Ensure the navigation panel does not unnecessarily reduce the editing workspace.

Provide a way to hide or show it.

## 16. Search and Replace

Implement functional document search.

Requirements:
- Search document text
- Highlight matches
- Navigate between matches
- Replace selected match
- Replace all matches
- Clear search

Search must operate on the document model.

Do not implement search as a fake input field.

## 17. Keyboard Shortcuts

Support common desktop word processor shortcuts.

Examples:
- Ctrl/Cmd + N: New document
- Ctrl/Cmd + O: Open
- Ctrl/Cmd + S: Save
- Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + S: Save as
- Ctrl/Cmd + Z: Undo
- Ctrl/Cmd + Y: Redo
- Ctrl/Cmd + B: Bold
- Ctrl/Cmd + I: Italic
- Ctrl/Cmd + U: Underline
- Ctrl/Cmd + F: Find
- Ctrl/Cmd + H: Replace
- Ctrl/Cmd + P: Print

Use the correct modifier conventions on each operating system.

Prevent shortcuts from interfering with normal text input.

## 18. Security

Follow secure desktop application practices.

Requirements:
- Use Tauri's security model.
- Minimize exposed backend commands.
- Validate filesystem operations.
- Avoid unrestricted filesystem access from the frontend.
- Use appropriate permissions.
- Avoid unsafe dynamic code execution.
- Do not store account credentials in plaintext.
- Do not expose authentication tokens unnecessarily.
- Do not embed secrets in frontend code.
- Handle external links safely.

Do not disable security features to simplify development.

## 19. Performance

The application should remain responsive.

Optimize:
- Document editing
- Large documents
- Toolbar updates
- Search
- File loading
- File saving
- Rendering
- Recovery

Avoid unnecessary rerenders.

Avoid expensive operations on every keystroke.

Use asynchronous operations where appropriate.

Do not block the application interface during document processing.

The application should be designed for practical use on ordinary desktop hardware.

## 20. Accessibility

Provide:
- Keyboard navigation
- Accessible control labels
- Visible focus states
- Readable typography
- Appropriate contrast
- Screen-reader-friendly controls
- Accessible menus
- Accessible dialogs

Do not make essential functionality mouse-only.

## 21. Commercial Product Requirements

Word-Client is intended to be a paid desktop application.

Design the architecture to support future commercial distribution.

Consider:
- Application versioning
- Release builds
- Cross-platform installers
- Update mechanisms
- License management
- Product settings
- Privacy
- Crash handling
- Documentation

Do not add fake payment functionality.

Do not add a fake subscription screen.

Do not block document editing behind a placeholder licensing system.

Do not invent a payment provider or implement a payment integration without explicit approval.

Keep licensing and payment functionality separate from the document editing engine.

The application must not depend on a remote server simply to open or edit local documents.

## 22. Testing

Test the application as a real desktop product.

Test:
- Application startup
- Application shutdown
- Creating documents
- Editing text
- Formatting
- Undo and redo
- Opening documents
- Saving documents
- Save as
- DOCX import
- DOCX export
- Reopening saved files
- Tables
- Images
- Search
- Keyboard shortcuts
- Theme switching
- Unsaved changes
- Recovery
- File permission errors
- Invalid files
- Window resizing

Test the platform-specific behavior on Linux, Windows, and macOS.

Do not claim that a platform has been tested if it has not.

If only Linux is available during development, document the untested Windows and macOS behavior.

## 23. Implementation Workflow

Follow this workflow:

Phase 1:
- Inspect the existing project.
- Establish the architecture.
- Identify dependencies.
- Create the desktop application foundation.

Phase 2:
- Build the main application window.
- Implement menus.
- Implement the document workspace.
- Implement themes.

Phase 3:
- Implement the structured editor.
- Implement core text formatting.
- Implement keyboard shortcuts.

Phase 4:
- Implement file operations.
- Implement DOCX import and export.
- Implement recovery.

Phase 5:
- Implement tables, images, search, and navigation.
- Improve document layout.

Phase 6:
- Implement platform-specific integration.
- Prepare Linux, Windows, and macOS packaging.

Phase 7:
- Test the application.
- Fix errors.
- Improve performance.
- Document limitations.

Do not stop after creating a visually convincing interface.

The application must have working functionality.

## 24. Final Requirements

The finished application must:

- Be named Word-Client.
- Be a real desktop application.
- Use Tauri 2.
- Use React and TypeScript.
- Use Tiptap/ProseMirror for structured editing.
- Support Linux, Windows, and macOS architecture.
- Support local document editing.
- Support DOCX import and export.
- Have a professional interface.
- Have light and dark themes.
- Have functional menus and toolbar controls.
- Use secure native filesystem operations.
- Be maintainable.
- Be suitable for future commercial distribution.

Prioritize correctness, document integrity, reliability, and actual functionality over superficial visual similarity.

Do not claim that features are complete unless they are implemented and tested.

Begin by inspecting the existing project and presenting a concise implementation plan. Then proceed with the implementation in logical stages.
